c.tagline: The French Riviera's glamorous yacht harbor, made famous by Brigitte Bardot and jet-set summers

card: Widely accepted, including at high-end beach clubs; cash useful for small vendors

taxi.fare: Metered, but often high fixed rates in peak season
taxi.fareNote: Taxis are expensive and scarce in high season; book ahead or use the seasonal shuttle boat from Sainte-Maxime

emergency.note: 112 is the general EU-style emergency number that connects to police, fire, and ambulance

english.label: Easy to get by in English

walk: The old town and port are compact and walkable; Pampelonne Beach is a few km out and best reached by bike, taxi, or the seasonal beach shuttle

safety.safety: Very safe town, though extremely crowded and expensive in peak summer
safety.crime: Petty theft near the port and beach clubs during peak season is the main concern

hood_landmark.Place des Lices: Place des Lices' plane-tree-shaded pétanque square and market
hood_landmark.Pampelonne Beach: Pampelonne Beach's row of exclusive beach clubs

avoid.reason: Pickpockets work the packed Vieux Port, Place des Lices market and beach clubs in July–August, and luxury-watch snatch thefts have targeted the flashy.

hood_desc: The glamorous yacht-lined harbor with cafes made for people-watching; the beating heart of Saint-Tropez.
The oldest, most photogenic quarter of pastel fishermen's houses and narrow lanes, quieter than the port.
A shaded square hosting the Saturday market and games of pétanque, ringed by cafes popular with locals.
A famous sweep of sandy beach a short drive south of town, lined with celebrity-favorite beach clubs and restaurants.

water.note: Tap water is safe to drink, though many visitors buy bottled for taste.

transit.sys: VarLib regional bus and seasonal shuttle boats across the Gulf of Saint-Tropez
transit.pay: Cash or contactless card on board; boat tickets purchased at the dock
transit.note: The seasonal boat shuttle from Sainte-Maxime avoids notorious summer road traffic into Saint-Tropez

transport.air: Nice Cote d'Azur Airport (NCE), about 1.5 hr away; Toulon-Hyeres Airport (TLN) is a closer alternative
transport.train: No direct rail; nearest stations are Saint-Raphael or Les Arcs-Draguignan, connected by bus
transport.bus: VarLib buses connect to Saint-Raphael, Toulon, and other Riviera towns
transport.ferry: Seasonal boats connect to Sainte-Maxime, Nice, and Cannes
transport.car: Notorious summer traffic jams on the approach roads; many visitors prefer the boat shuttle

airport.name: Nice Cote d'Azur Airport
airport.transport: Shuttle bus/transfer, or helicopter transfer in peak season

net.w: Free wifi standard in hotels and cafes
net.ap: An Orange, SFR, or Bouygues tourist SIM or eSIM

tip.s: Not obligatory; rounding up is appreciated
tip.r: Service is included by law, though rounding up is common at upscale restaurants and beach clubs

food.name: Tarte tropezienne
food.desc: Sugar-crusted brioche split and filled with a cream of pastry cream and buttercream, created here in 1955 and named by Brigitte Bardot on a film set.

places.name: La Tarte Tropezienne
places.note: The original bakery from the recipe's creator; buy individual sizes or a whole cake.

places.name: Senequier
places.note: The red-awning harbour cafe since 1887; a slice with coffee watching the yachts.

places.name: Patisserie Cavazza
places.note: Village patisserie whose version locals rate against the famous one.

food.name: Bouillabaisse
food.desc: Provencal fisherman's stew of rockfish, scorpion fish and conger simmered with saffron, fennel and tomato, served as broth then fish, with rouille croutons.

places.name: Le Girelier
places.note: Harbour-front seafood house of more than 50 years; bouillabaisse is its signature.

places.name: Chez Camille
places.note: Beachside institution just outside town; book well ahead in summer.

places.name: La Petite Plage
places.note: Mediterranean seafood on the quay, with whole fish and shellfish platters.

food.name: Salade nicoise
food.desc: Tomato, egg, olives, anchovy or tuna, radish and raw broad beans dressed in olive oil. Purists on this coast leave out potato and green beans entirely.

places.name: Le Cafe
places.note: Village square terrace beside the boules pitch; a fixture since 1789.

places.name: Bar du Port
places.note: All-day harbour terrace, reliable for a light Provencal lunch.

places.name: Auberge des Maures
places.note: Saint-Tropez's oldest restaurant, in a vine-shaded courtyard off the lanes.

food.name: Soupe au pistou
food.desc: Late-summer vegetable and bean soup finished at the table with a spoonful of basil, garlic and olive oil pounded in a mortar. Never contains pine nuts here.

places.name: Le Sporting
places.note: Unpretentious brasserie locals use year-round, off the yacht-crowd circuit.

places.name: La Ponche
places.note: Hotel restaurant in the old fishermen's quarter, cooking classic Provencal plates.

places.name: Chez Fuchs
places.note: First-floor old-town bistro, a genuinely Tropezien room above a tobacconist.

food.name: Grilled loup de mer
food.desc: Sea bass or daurade from the gulf, grilled whole over fennel branches, boned at the table and dressed with nothing more than olive oil and lemon.

places.name: Le Girelier
places.note: Choose your fish by weight from the display; grilled simply, priced by the kilo.

places.name: Chez Fuchs
places.note: Old-school kitchen that treats a whole fish with restraint.

places.name: La Petite Plage
places.note: Day-boat catch listed on the board, cooked plainly and well.

food.name: Beignets de fleurs de courgette
food.desc: Courgette flowers picked the same morning, dipped in a light batter and fried until they blister. A short-lived Provencal early-summer treat.

places.name: Auberge des Maures
places.note: Seasonal starters straight from the Place des Lices market a few streets away.

places.name: La Table du Marche
places.note: Market-driven bistro and deli from a well-known local chef.

places.name: Place des Lices market
places.note: Tuesday and Saturday market; growers sell the flowers and stalls fry them fresh.

food.name: Cotes de Provence rose
food.desc: Pale, dry and barely pink, the wine this coast built. Drunk cold from noon onwards, usually from a vineyard within sight of the village.

places.name: Chateau Minuty
places.note: Classified estate minutes from town, with tastings and cellar-door sales.

places.name: Domaine Bertaud Belieu
places.note: Large neighbouring estate on the peninsula; easy visit and generous tasting.

places.name: Senequier
places.note: The most-photographed terrace in town for a chilled glass at sunset.

food.name: Pastis
food.desc: Anise spirit poured over ice and cut five to one with cold water until it clouds. The pre-lunch and pre-dinner ritual of the whole Var coast.

places.name: Le Gorille Cafe
places.note: Long-running quayside cafe, open early and late, popular with locals off-season.

places.name: Le Sporting
places.note: Zinc bar where the boules players come in for a pastis after a game.

places.name: Le Cafe
places.note: Order one on the terrace and watch the petanque; boules are lent to guests.

landmarks: Vieux Port (Old Port)
The legendary harbour where gleaming superyachts moor before ochre fishermen's houses, its quayside cafes the epicentre of Riviera people-watching.
La Ponche
The old fishing quarter of narrow lanes, pastel facades and hidden coves where Brigitte Bardot-era bohemia still lingers behind the glamour.
Citadelle de Saint-Tropez
A 17th-century hilltop fortress with roaming peacocks, housing the maritime history museum and the finest views over town, gulf and Maures hills.
Place des Lices
The quintessential Provençal square where locals play pétanque beneath plane trees and the twice-weekly market spills over with linen, antiques and tapenade.
Église Notre-Dame de l'Assomption
Saint-Tropez's ochre-and-terracotta bell tower, the town's postcard symbol, sheltering the bust of local patron Saint Torpes paraded during the Bravade.
Musée de l'Annonciade
A deconsecrated 16th-century chapel on the port holding a stellar collection of Signac, Matisse and the Pointillists who made Saint-Tropez an artists' haven.
Musée de la Gendarmerie et du Cinéma
The famous gendarmerie station from the Louis de Funès comedies, reborn as a playful museum of Saint-Tropez's starring role in cinema history.
Plage de Pampelonne
The mythical five-kilometre sweep of sand in nearby Ramatuelle, birthplace of the Riviera beach-club scene since And God Created Woman.
Sentier du Littoral (Coastal Path)
A gorgeous shoreline trail rounding the peninsula from the Graniers beach past secret coves, lighthouses and umbrella pines to Cap Camarat.
Phare de Saint-Tropez
A stone lighthouse built in 1866 at the tip of the harbor breakwater, its beam still guiding yachts past the crowded Vieux Port.

train.note: Saint-Tropez has no railway - the branch line closed in 1948. The nearest station is Saint-Raphaël-Valescure, about 35 km east, on the Mediterranean main line with TGV services to Paris and TER trains along the coast; from there take the bus or the seasonal boat. SNCF fares open around six months ahead (https://www.sncf-connect.com/en-en/).

bus.note: No international coaches. Zou! bus line 876 runs from Saint-Raphaël station to Saint-Tropez in about 90 minutes along a road that gridlocks completely in July and August - the boat is often faster. Buses also serve Ramatuelle, Gassin and Sainte-Maxime. Long-distance FlixBus services stop at Saint-Raphaël rather than Saint-Tropez.

intl.to: Sainte-Maxime & Port Grimaud (France) - across the gulf, ~15-20 min

ferry.note: The boats are genuinely the smart way to arrive - the Sainte-Maxime shuttle runs year-round and takes 15 minutes against an hour or more by road in season, and the Saint-Raphaël service connects with the trains. Sailings are seasonal on the longer routes, roughly April to October, and are cancelled in strong mistral winds. Boats dock right in the old port.

half.name: Port Grimaud
half.blurb: A Venice-like 1960s lagoon village of canals, bridges and pastel cottages at the head of the gulf, best admired from a coche d'eau boat.
